We show that our model can reduce the mechanistic hypothesis space by showing, e.g., that C–C coupling happens via the *CO adsorbates rather than atomic carbon, and it points to missing physics at high CO pressures, such as multiple site types or CO transport near the active sites. Our bimodal strategy balances theoretical and experimental insights, paving the way toward a new mechanistic understanding and catalytic design concepts for next-generation electrolyzers.

item.title: Computational Drug Discovery of Natural Product Compounds for Tyrosinase Inhibition
item.description: Plants produce chemically diverse compounds for defence and survival, many of which exhibit biological activity and offer promising starting points for drug discovery. This study thus investigated natural compounds as potential inhibitors of tyrosinase, a key enzyme in melanin production and an established target in the treatment of hyperpigmentation. A quantitative structure–activity relationship (QSAR) machine-learning model was developed using ChEMBL tyrosinase bioactivity data and property-matched decoys. Ten models, including decision trees, random forests and gradient boosting, were evaluated; logistic regression was selected for virtual screening. To make the model generalise to unseen chemistry, the model was tested on compounds that were required to have Tanimoto similarity of 0.40 or less to every training compound and to share no Bemis–Murcko scaffold with them. The model achieved an AUC of 0.82 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.78–0.86), compared with 0.56 using physicochemical properties alone. The frozen model was then used to screen 404,570 natural products from COCONUT (COlleCtion of Open Natural prodUcTs) and IMPPAT (Indian Medicinal Plants, Phytochemistry And Therapeutics). Of the top 1% of predictions, 1,694 compounds were both structurally novel and represented new scaffolds. Following computational filters for predicted skin permeability and potentially reactive chemical groups indicating skin irritation, the 100 highest-scoring candidates were selected for molecular docking. Docking reproduced the crystallographic tropolone binding pose with a root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) of 1.20 Å, while the most predictive docking score achieved an AUC of 0.64 (95% CI, 0.61–0.66). Among the ten highest-ranked candidates, two were associated with Anisomeles indica (Indian catmint) and two with Phaseolus lunatus (lima beans). These candidates warrant experimental validation and further investigation for potential dermatological applications.

item.title: Tunable Oxygen Evolution Activity on the Lanthanum Oxide Terminated Perovskites
item.description: Electronic structure descriptors have been widely used to predict the oxygen evolution reaction (OER) activity. Herein, the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) is used to predict active LaO-terminated LaBO3 (B = Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu) perovskites for the OER. Density functional theory calculations show that the adsorption free energies of ∗O on La–La sites are correlated with the HOMO. In contrast, the Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni and Cu sites of the BO2 termination show a weaker dependence on the HOMO. Changes in the magnetic moment show that the La–La sites are non-oxidisable, so the electrons are taken from the surrounding perovskite. The B sites are oxidisable and provide the electrons locally. Comparing the theoretical overpotential with the HOMO, a volcano-type trend is shown for the La–La sites, which is not observed on the B sites. A composition-based model predicts active LaO-terminated LaCo1−xCuxO3. Finally, a correlation is shown between the experimental OER overpotentials from three independent studies in the literature and the computed HOMO.

item.title: A Versatile (Photo)Electrochemical Array with Temperature, Illumination and Mass Transport Control for Measurements from Molecules to Microorganisms
item.description: The growth in (photo)electroactive materials development creates a demand for platforms that can systematically measure and compare (photo)electrochemical reactions. Existing electrochemical screening platforms offer limited control over experimental parameters and the range of samples that can be assessed. Here, we developed a versatile multi-well electrochemical array platform that offers programmable control of illumination, temperature, and convection. The platform incorporates a programmable stage that automates plate positioning and electrode washing to minimize cross-contamination between measurements. The sample plates can accommodate customizable electrodes and have been designed to fit into plate readers, allowing complementary optical analyses. Eight wells are measured simultaneously, and the full plate (with 24-wells) is screened in three successive rounds. Electrochemical consistency across the array was validated by cyclic voltammetry of [Fe(CN)6]3−/4−, with 0.13% carryover between successive measurements. Reproducible chopped-light photocurrents were obtained from the photoactive molecules [Ru(bpy)3]2+ and methylene blue under different LED wavelengths and calibrated light intensities. Lastly, currents from the photosynthetic cyanobacterium Synechocystis sp. PCC 6803 were measured across a large range of conditions, including applied potential, temperature, stirring, and mediator concentration, to systematically identify the conditions for optimal photocurrent output. Notably, parallel electrochemical mediator screening was completed in one day, compared with an estimated 12 days for the sequential workflow. This study establishes a much-needed analytical platform that reproducibly generates high-quality photoelectrochemical data from diverse photoactive materials, accelerating the discovery of high-performance systems.A multi-well (photo)electrochemical array with programmable control of illumination, temperature, and convection, enables parallel and reproducible measurements of samples ranging from electroactive molecules to living photosynthetic microorganisms.

item.title: CertMat: Formally Certified Robust Phase and Elastic Stability Verification Across One Million Inorganic Crystals
item.description: Machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) and high-throughput density functional theory (DFT) workflows have expanded candidate inorganic crystal catalogs to the million-material scale, yet thermodynamic convex hull stability (Ehull = 0) and mechanical Born stability (C ≻ 0) remain evaluated almost exclusively via floating-point point estimates that neglect energy and stiffness uncertainties. Here we introduce CertMat, an exact rational certificate generator and machine-checked Lean 4 formal verification kernel (leanprover/lean4:v4.16.0, zero Mathlib dependencies, zero sorry or non-standard axioms across 51 mechanized theorems) that certifies worst-case phase and elastic stability over heterogeneous uncertainty boxes. CertMat mechanizes four core theorem families: (1) exact Farkas primal-dual soundness with non-negative margin enforcement (δ ≥ 0) for convex hull decompositions, (2) exact algebraic cancellation of correlated elemental reference-state errors ( ∑ e cieδµe) proving that only uncorrelated residual errors (ηi) can flip phase stability, (3) universal worst-case interval robustness over heterogeneous energy boxes Ei ∈ [Li, Ui] with an exact Charnes–Cooper linear-fractional solver for the critical destabilization radius ε∗(x) and adversarial decomposition Phase Switching, and (4) exact rational LDLT Born positive-definiteness, constructive non-PD strain counterexamples, Voigt Frobenius–Weyl robustness and constructive rank-1 fragility witnesses, and bidirectional pure-rational SO(3)-invariant Mandel/Kelvin Frobenius–Weyl robustness and constructive rank-1 fragility theorems (requiring no irrational √ 2). Auditing 1,044,460 unique crystal phase entries (plus 234,086 matched PBE–r2SCAN sub-hull re-audits, totaling 1,278,545 competed LP audits and 1 uncompeted elemental phase) and 34,323 valid 6 × 6 elastic tensors across Google DeepMind GNoME (PBE and r2SCAN), NIST JARVIS-DFT 3D, and Matbench Discovery WBM—with 95,348 / 95,348 serialized TSV rational certificates machine-verified by the compiled Lean 4 certmat-check binary and an independent pure-Fraction checker (0 failures) plus 540/540 stratified spot-audit dataset-binding checks—we establish four major findings: (i) on 117,043 matched GNoME PBE-vs-r2SCAN crystals, correlated elemental shifts explain R2 = 73.51% of formation-energy discrepancies (reducing MAE from 78.90 to 30.96 meV/atom), and CertMat’s worst-case Fragile classification separates real r2SCAN stability flips with 24.65x relative risk (0.46% vs. 11.36% flip rate, ROC-AUC 0.8948) on exact 117k matched sub-hulls and 5.10x relative risk (96.40% recall) on GNoME’s primary external Decomposition Energy Per Atom column (6.20x relative risk / 97.46% recall on ... MP); (ii) 11,481 of 34,323 (33.45%) valid JARVIS-DFT 3D elastic tensors fail exact Born stability with Lean-certified rational strain witnesses, while 2,643 (11.57%) of Born-PD crystals are fragile under unconstrained 5 GPa Voigt perturbations (Lean-certified via WEYL_FRAGILE) and 1,517 (6.64%) are fragile under SO(3)-invariant 5 GPa Mandel perturbations (bidirectional Lean certification: 22,531 MANDEL_ WEYL_ROBUST + 3,198 MANDEL_WEYL_FRAGILE witnesses); (iii) 19,894 of 42,688 (46.60%) WBM candidates reported stable against the static MP2020 hull collapse to strictly unstable under intra-catalog WBM competition alone (62.19% via same-composition polymorphs, 37.81% via cross-composition decomposition; 40.80% even after unique-prototype deduplication); and (iv) our exact hull audit uncovered a pervasive upstream unit-scaling defect in the published NIST JARVIS-DFT 3D Figshare release (jdft_3d-9-24-2025.json) consistent with dividing per-atom optb88vdw_total_energy a second time by reduced formula-unit atom count Nfu, inflating ehull > 1.0 eV/atom for 63,386 materials (median residual 0.00677 eV vs. 2.605 and 2.108 eV for two negative controls). Code, Lean 4 proofs, and full verification artifacts are publicly available at https://github.com/sunpunggi1/certmat.

item.title: Nonempirical Double-hybrid Functionals Entering the AI Field: the Adaptative LS1DH model
item.description: We introduce a machine-learning-assisted nonempirical double-hybrid density-functional approximation, dubbed adaptative LS1DH or aLS1DH, which combines the theoretical constraints of the linearly scaled one-parameter double-hybrid (LS1DH) model with system-specific flexibility. Based on kernel ridge regression (KRR) and convolutional many-body distribution function (cMBDF) representations, aLS1DH predicts optimal system-dependent fractions of nonlocal exchange and correlation while preserving size consistency. Its performance is assessed on the extended GMTKN55 and on the recently developed CYCLO70. The aLS1DH model consistently improves upon its parent functional, PBE0-DH, rivaling the latest machine-learning-based functionals such as skala functional. These results highlight the potential of machine learning to improve the accuracy of nonempirical double hybrids while retaining their underlying theoretical constraints.

item.title: Chemistry decides the calibration unit: five direct and one water-mediated interaction class
item.description: Typed protein–ligand contact models predict which interactions form, but they return point probabilities, not a statement of how often the true contact is included. We formulate per-atom, multi-label interaction sets for five direct contact classes (H-bond, hydrophobic, π, salt, halogen) and add water as a sixth, water-mediated class. Using cross-conformal calibration and conformal risk control on 750 crystal complexes across 29 targets, we show that the calibration unit is a chemical decision rather than a statistical default. At the 90% nominal level a chemistry-aware nonconformity score reduces set size by 7.9% (target-held-out) and 13.2% (scaffold-held-out), changing coverage by only +0.6/−0.6 percentage points. Per-type risk control attains false-negative rates of 0.096/0.079 at a 10% target, but only for classes with enough calibration positives: salt has 42 positives and is not estimable, while π is under-covered by a global threshold. Water is abundant (1,258 positives; 5.4% of ligand heavy atoms; 72% of complexes) and target-specific. A global threshold on the probability score leaves water at 0.905/0.937/0.931/0.853 coverage on target/scaffold/temporal/strict splits, but the original chemistry-aware score is water-blind by construction and drops to 0.735/0.751/0.750/0.635. Making the partner term water-aware recovers only 0.848/0.877/0.886/0.787, while per-type control gives 0.923/0.937/0.928/0.857. Per-type control is therefore not a universal winner: it fixes π and water, can lower halogen, and cannot estimate salt. The calibration unit should follow the chemistry of the class, not an aggregate coverage target.

item.title: When Nondetects Decide the Verdict: Left-Censored Data Handling and Compliance Decision Errors under Extreme Censoring
item.description: Compliance assessments commonly replace nondetects with zero, half, or the full reporting limit. We asked how often this choice, not the data, determines whether a 95th percentile (P95) or mean exceeds a regulatory limit. In a pre-specified simulation spanning 20–99% nondetects, structural zeros, and 30–1000 samples, we evaluated decision errors of substitution, nonparametric, censored-likelihood, and Bayesian methods. With one reporting limit, lower- and upper-bound substitution rarely disagreed at ≤80% nondetects but in 53–61% of data sets at 95% when the reporting limit exceeded the regulatory limit. In a screening reanalysis of the Fifth Unregulated Contaminant Monitoring Rule (UCMR 5), substitution alone determined whether 458 PFOA and 406 PFOS systems were classified as exceeding maximum contaminant levels at the reporting limit. In simulations of this case, lower-bound substitution missed exceedances despite more sampling. In exploratory analyses, no eligible method kept both error rates ≤20% with 30 samples for most nondetect proportions. For upper-limit decisions, the best method needed roughly 300–400 samples at ≤95% nondetects, largely reflecting the narrow decision margin, and none sufficed with up to 1000 at 99%. Under extreme censoring, data often cannot identify the decision. The remedy is more samples or lower reporting limits, not a better estimator.

item.title: Downstream purification route influences the viscoelastic properties of silk-elastin-like polypeptide hydrogels
item.description: The development of novel recombinant protein-based materials requires a bottom-up understanding of sequence-processing-property relationships. However, most studies have focused on how the amino acid sequence determines material properties, whereas the effect of downstream purification (DSP) remains largely unexplored. Here, we compare two silk-elastin-like polypeptides (SELPs) with different molecular weight (MW) and clustering of silk-like blocks. Each SELP was purified by two different DSP routes: inverse temperature cycling (ITC) or ammonium sulfate precipitation (ASP). Using a combination of experiments and molecular simulations, we show that the DSP route affects hydrogel formation and viscoelastic properties in a sequence-dependent manner. The low MW SELP was insensitive to the DSP route, whereas ITC of high MW SELPs led to irreversible hydrogel formation and with a 2-fold higher storage modulus than ASP. Our multiscale characterisation suggested that DSP influences how readily silk-like blocks form intermolecular βsheet crosslinks as a function of the DSP route. These results indicate that SELP hydrogel properties can be modulated not only by sequence design, but also through the DSP route applied, which has implications on cost and efficiency for designing scalable SELP biomanufacturing processes.

item.title: Learning to Smell: Representing Olfaction with Artificial Intelligence
item.description: Olfaction plays a fundamental role in how humans perceive and interact with their chemical environment, yet predicting how odors are perceived remains a major scientific challenge. Artificial intelligence (AI) has advanced odor prediction, but its capabilities depend critically on how chemical and perceptual information is represented and learned. In this review, we examine how different molecular representations shape both the predictive capabilities and scientific insights of AI models for olfaction. We discuss the progression from predefined molecular descriptors to learned representations and biologically anchored models incorporating odorant receptor information, highlighting what each approach can capture and where its limitations lie. We further examine challenges in predicting complex odor mixtures, concentration-dependent responses, and individual differences in perception, as well as the scarcity and heterogeneity of experimental data. We propose data integration and biologically informed representation learning as opportunities to improve generalization and help connect molecular recognition with olfactory perception. Finally, we argue that future progress should be measured not only by predictive accuracy but also by AI models' ability to generate experimentally testable insights into the mechanisms of olfaction.

item.title: Accurate, Rapid, and High-Throughput Photophysical Determination of Critical Micelle Concentrations of Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances
item.description: Aggregation is a defining yet poorly characterized physicochemical behavior of many per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), influencing their environmental fate, interfacial partitioning, and treatment performance. Critical micelle concentration (CMC) is a key physicochemical parameter describing PFAS aggregation; however, CMC data remain limited, and existing measurement approaches are often labor-intensive, PFAS-consuming, low-throughput, or dependent on specialized instrumentation. Here, we develop and validate a photophysical assay for PFAS CMC determination leveraging microplate reader technology. The assay provides three independent yet consistent readouts, fluorescence emission, UV-vis absorbance, and fluorescence polarization, enabling robust CMC determination with minimal sample consumption. Using perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) as a model compound, the assay yielded CMC values in excellent agreement with conventional conductivity and 19F NMR measurements. Application of the assay to a diverse set of PFAS revealed the influence of molecular structure and head-group chemistry on aggregation behavior. Temperature-dependent measurements further demonstrated chain-length-dependent micellization trends, while environmentally relevant solution conditions showed minimal effects of natural organic matter but pronounced impacts of ionic strength, cation valency, and PFAS mixture composition. Together, these results provide systematic experimental evaluation of PFAS aggregation behavior, revealing how PFAS species and environmental chemistry govern micellization while establishing a scalable platform for PFAS physicochemical characterization.

item.title: All-Optical Nuclear Spin Hyperpolarization via Spin Level Anti-Crossing of Pentacene Transient Triplet State
item.description: We demonstrate all-optical nuclear spin hyperpolarization in pentacene-doped naphthalene single crystals via the spin level anti-crossing (SLAC) of photoexcited triplet states. Using pulsed laser excitation alone without microwave irradiation, we obtain a bulk 1H polarization of ∼0.4% at 80 K near the SLAC (∼12.5 mT), corresponding to an enhancement of ∼ 2.5×104. The polarization arises from state mixing driven by the zero-field splitting and hyperfine interactions in the laboratory frame. The magnitude and orientation of the field tune the energy gap between the two triplet sublevels at the SLAC. For molecules aligned with the field, this gap can match the nuclear Larmor frequency, analogous to the solid effect (SE) in dynamic nuclear polarization (DNP). Misalignment can widen the energy gap beyond the nuclear Larmor frequency at all fields, in which case polarization arises from state mixing analogous to resonant-mixing (RM) DNP. The unexpected field profile is explained by a small distribution of molecular orientations. We further show that magnetic-field modulation synchronized with the laser pulses increases the polarization and accelerates its build-up similar to the integrated solid effect. These results establish an efficient, robust and microwave-free route to nuclear hyperpolarization and all-optical control of electron-nuclear spin systems.

item.title: Beyond Shape: Odorant Conformational Ensembles Encode Topology, Molecular Size, and Polar-Surface Coherence
item.description: Odor is widely modelled as three-dimensional shape recognition: a flexible odorant presents a 300 K conformer ensemble to a receptor repertoire, implying that perceptual breadth peaks at an intermediate number of accessible shapes and that explicit 3D representations outperform 2D molecular graphs. We test both predictions under a cryptographically pre-registered plan across catalogue profiles (n = 4,808), human psychophysics (n = 304) and heterologous receptor arrays (n = 294). Computing 300 K GFN2-xTB ensembles at a 200-conformer ceiling for all 1,821 flexible cohort members (106,526 conformers) and benchmarking 21 neural representations across 10 seeds, we find that neither claim holds. Conformational entropy saturates by 28 conformers (88% attained at a ceiling of 20), excluding an interior breadth optimum sixfold below the populated range (β2 = +0.0080, 95% CI -0.0014 to +0.0172). No 3D representation outperforms a capacity-matched or descriptor-augmented 2D graph. Out-of-sample-replicated confound analyses show that 3D shape dispersion vanishes once chain topology is controlled; instead, breadth reflects coarse topological flexibility (peaking at 9.2 rotatable bonds), molecular extent and polar-surface coherence (concave β2 = -0.0264). Keywords: conformational ensemble · odor breadth · molecular representation · Artificial Intelligence · Graph Neural Network

item.title: A Foundation Model for Accurate Atomistic Simulations in Drug Design
item.description: Artificial intelligence has revolutionized the prediction of static protein structures, but characterizing their dynamics and their interactions with drug candidates remains a computational bottleneck. Simulations that address this challenge need both the accuracy of quantum chemistry and the speed to reach biologically relevant timescales. To meet these requirements, we introduce FeNNix-Bio1, a fast and scalable foundation machine-learning potential trained primarily on high-accuracy quantum chemistry data, which enables reactive atomistic simulations of biological systems. Here, we show that FeNNix-Bio1 captures subtle condensed-phase phenomena such as ion solvation and the properties of liquid water, predicts the hydration free energies of more than 600 small molecules and the absolute binding free energies of 30 protein-ligand complexes in good agreement with experiment, and describes protein structure and dynamics, lipid bilayers and chemical reactions, in simulations of up to more than a million atoms.

item.title: Boltz-GenFree: structure-generation-free ranking for first-stage affinity screening
item.description: Boltz-2 predicts affinity from a structure it generates for every candidate, which makes library-scale screening expensive, and several studies suggest that this pose contributes little to the predicted affinity. We tested this with fine-grained interventions and built Boltz-GenFree, which predicts affinity without building a structure for any candidate, generated or docked. On its own it keeps 90% of the Boltz-2 mean AP, against 67% for Boltzina, and combined with Boltz-2 in a simulated two-stage screen, in which only the top 10% of its ranking is re-ranked, it matches the mean AP of Boltz-2 alone on eight libraries (0.0839 against 0.0840) at an estimated 8.5 to 8.9 times lower cost. Its cheap ranking can thus decide where to spend the expensive steps, whether the shortlist re-ranked by Boltz-2 or the 300 labels used for fine-tuning, which raised AP on seven of eight targets.

item.title: 4-Pyridylidene Bisiminothiolate Nickel Complexes as Structural and Functional Models of the Enzyme-Bound Nickel Pincer Nucleotide
item.description: Lactate racemase (LarA) and a recently discovered family of hydride transferases use the nickel pincer nucleotide (NPN) cofactor to shuttle a hydride to and from their substrates. The 4‑pyridylidene SCS pincer ligand of this cofactor is proposed to accept the hydride at the C4 position through a proton-coupled hydride transfer (PCHT) mechanism. Herein, we report a series of SCS nickel complexes supported by N-alkyl secondary thioamide pincer ligands (R = adamantyl, benzhydryl) as structural and functional models of this metallocofactor. Metalation with NiI2 affords an inseparable mixture of the monomer (H1SCSR)NiI, which carries an unsymmetrical thioamide/iminothiolate donor pair, and the neutral trimer [(SCSR)Ni]3, in which both arms are iminothiolates. Coordinating bases convert both species to the fully deprotonated adducts (SCSR)Ni(L) (L = N-benzylimidazole, NBIz; 1,1,3,3-tetramethylguanidine, TMG). The NBIz complex reproduces the C,S,S,N(imidazole) donor set and square planar geometry of the histidine-bound NPN cofactor, and its electronic absorption features are reminiscent of those reported for LarA. DFT calculations locate the LUMO on the pyridylidene ring with substantial density at C4. In combination with TMG, (SCSR)Ni(NBIz) catalyzes the racemization of lactic acid and related α-hydroxy carboxylic acids (TON up to ca. 8), and in situ studies identify (SCSR)Ni(tmg) as the resting state with no evidence for lactate coordination to nickel. Treatment with NBu4BH4 generates new absorptions comparable to those of the reported 1,4- and 1,2-dihydropyridinate complexes and of NaBH4-treated LarA, consistent with hydride addition at the C4 and/or C2 positions. Overall, these results align with a ligand-centered PCHT pathway and extend the racemization activity of synthetic NPN models from thiocarboxylate to thioamide-derived SCS pincer ligands.

item.title: AtomTrans: A Plane-Wave-Based Computational Platform for Electron and Phonon Quantum Transport with Atom-Anchored Wannier Functions
item.description: We present AtomTrans, a computational platform for coherent electron and harmonic phonon transport based on plane-wave density-functional theory. AtomTrans combines systematic control of the plane-wave basis with atom-labelled Wannier functions for open-boundary calculations. Projectability-guided disentanglement selects the electronic subspace, and Löwdin orthonormalization of projected atomic trial orbitals yields atom-labelled Wannier functions. Electrode blocks extracted from device buffers share a common gauge and energy reference with the scattering region. AtomTrans applies the same partitioning scheme and Green’s-function solver to the electronic Hamiltonian and an independently calculated dynamical matrix. The software calculates transmission, total and projected densities of states, real-space local density of states, and thermoelectric coefficients. Finite-bias currents are evaluated using either the fixed equilibrium transmission or a self-consistent electrostatic treatment. Comparisons with QuantumATK cover three representative systems. For an Au–benzenedithiolate–Au junction, we examine molecular resonances, spatial distributions, and the current–voltage response. Compared with the rigid-transmission approximation, electrostatic self-consistency reduces high-bias current deviations from QuantumATK. The relative deviations are at most 3.1% at ±1.8 and ±2.0 V. For an armchair graphene nanoribbon, phonon thermal conductances agree within 4% at 300–900 K, and both software packages yield a peak thermoelectric figure of merit of 0.19 at 300 K. For an Au–Co–Au chain, the minority-spin antiresonance is highly sensitive to the LCAO basis, whereas increasing the plane-wave cutoff from 400 to 800 eV shifts its position by only 0.01 eV. These results demonstrate AtomTrans’s capabilities for charge and heat transport and illustrate the systematic control of plane-wave basis convergence in spin-dependent transport.

item.title: Transition-Metal-Free Amination of Aryl Halides via Facile Aryne Generation
item.description: Despite continued advances in transition-metal-catalyzed amination of aryl halides, persistent challenges, including costly scale-up, sensitivity to steric hindrance, and catalyst poisoning by heteroaromatic rings, necessitate the development of metal-free alternatives. Aryne intermediates are an attractive option due to their high reactivity, yet facile aryne generation from aryl halides remains a formidable challenge. Herein, we disclose a transition-metal-free amination strategy for aryl halides that uses KHMDS with an 18-crown-6 additive, proceeding via aryne intermediates. The reactions use exclusively commercial reagents, proceed at room temperature, and achieve near “dump-and-stir” simplicity for reaction setup. The methodology is applicable to a wide range of aryl and heteroaryl halides with excellent chemoselectivity, including (S)-3,3′-dibromo-2,2′dimethoxy-BINOL and strongly Lewis basic substrates such as quinoline and pyrimidine that typically impede Pd-catalyzed aminations. Both primary and secondary amines participate, including sterically hindered 1-adamantylamine and diisopropylamine, providing a basis for preparative scale synthesis and evaluation of medicinally relevant aryl halides and amines.

item.title: Influences of Surface Reconstruction and Iron-Associated Activation of Nickel-Based Electrocatalysts on Oxygen Evolution Reaction
item.description: Ni-based electrocatalysts are among state-of-the-arts for oxygen evolution reaction (OER) in alkaline media, and their interaction with Fe impurities in the electrolyte is widely understood as an origin of the enhanced catalytic performance. The surface of these catalysts undergoes physicochemical changes in electrochemical operation environments, and this reconstruction of surface is intertwined with the Fe-associated promotion of activity. However, these two phenomena have often been understood together, and their influences were difficult to be comprehended separately. Herein, we used SrNiO3 and LaNiO3 as model catalysts with different surface-reconstruction behaviors. By examining their characteristics in the absence and present of Fe in the electrolyte, importance of the access to Fe species in the electrolyte could be unveiled. Based on systematic investigations, we then found out that the interaction between the Fe and the catalyst surface under active reconstruction (during the initial stage of operation) might lead to a negative contribution to the overall OER activity. To resolve this issue, we suggest a simple strategy to maximize the catalytic performance; inducing the surface reconstruction in the absence of Fe, followed by exposure of the catalyst to Fe in the electrolyte for the promotion of OER. Around two-fold increase in the performance were achieved in optimized conditions, though identical catalysts were used, and the versatility of our approach was verified by applying the same strategy to Ni hydroxides.

item.title: Superhydrophobic Surfaces Across the Agri-Food Continuum: Mechanisms, Multifunctional Antifouling, Water-Saving Operations, and Sustainable Pathways from Pre-Harvest to Post-Harvest Systems
item.description: Interfacial fouling across agricultural production and food processing drives foodborne illness, post-harvest spoilage, excessive water and chemical consumption, and energy losses. Superhydrophobic surfaces—characterized by static water contact angles exceeding 150° and sliding angles below 10°—offer a unifying physical and chemical defense across the pre-harvest to post-harvest continuum. This review critically evaluates advances predominantly from 2023 to 2026 in superhydrophobic and wetting-engineered coatings targeting bacterial biofilms, fungal spores, soil and mud adhesion, viscous liquid food residues, thermal dairy fouling, and pipeline drag or scaling. Mechanistic developments linking Cassie–Baxter plastron stability and stochastic extended Derjaguin–Landau–Verwey–Overbeek modeling to multi-foulant repulsion are integrated with pre-harvest field applications, metallic and polymeric food contact surfaces, edible produce coatings, water-saving clean-in-place operations, and drip irrigation hydraulics. Finally, mechanical durability, evaluation beyond static contact angle, migration toxicology, and fluorine-free regulatory pathways replacing per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances and microplastics are assessed.

item.title: Ascorbate Peroxidase (APEX2) Activates Dihydrotetrazine Oxidation for Rapid Bioorthogonal Chemistry in Living Cells
item.description: It is shown that genetically expressible APEX2 efficiently catalyzes the oxidation of dihydrotetrazine (DHTz) to give tetrazine products that engage in rapid bioorthogonal reactions with trans-cyclooctene dienophiles. Through in vitro studies, it is shown that the APEX2-catalyzed DHTz oxidation is accelerated by superoxide dismutase— an enzyme found in all mammalian cells that regulates oxidative stress by disproportioning superoxide into O2 and H2O2. While the addition of H2O2 is not required for APEX2-catalyzed DHTz oxidation, the catalytic efficiency is increased substantially to kcat/KM 4.90 × 103 M–1s–1 by the addition of a small amount of H2O2 (10 μM). These ‘minimal peroxide’ conditions are mild compared to the higher H2O2 concentrations that are typically employed in phenolic oxidation reactions promoted by APEX2. APEX2's ability to promote DHTz oxidation for subsequent Diels-Alder chemistry was demonstrated in live HeLa cells transiently transfected with cytosolic GFP-HaloTag-APEX2 (GHA), a fusion protein containing a fluorescent reporter, a self-labeling domain for dihydrotetrazine conjugation, and a catalytic domain, respectively. Alternatively, enzyme-catalyzed intracellular DHTz oxidation was promoted using separate plasmids and a dual-transfection protocol to introduce APEX2 and the HaloTag-anchor for DHTz.Upon oxidation, the resulting tetrazine was conjugated in situ to a fluorophore-tagged TCO, and conjugation efficiency was assayed through in-gel fluorescence, western blot analysis, and confocal microscopy. In live PC3 cells, it was further shown that APEX2 catalyzed the oxidation of a DHTz that had been selectively conjugated to endogenous monoacylglycerol lipase (MAGL) via a selective covalent warhead.

item.title: Ligand-Controlled Regiodivergent Boracarboxylation of 1,2-Dienes Using Carbon Dioxide and Copper Catalysts
item.description: Regiodivergent transformations are powerful tools in organic synthesis, enabling the divergent construction of desired products from a single substrate. While regiodivergent functionalization has been studied, regiodivergent carboxylation utilizing carbon dioxide remains limited. We herein report a regiodivergent Cu-catalyzed boracarboxylation of 1,2dienes. By simply tuning the phosphine ligands, the regiochemical outcome can be strictly controlled: the use of PCy3 affords borylated alpha,beta-unsaturated carboxylates, whereas PtBu3 yields the corresponding beta,gamma-unsaturated isomers with high regioselectivity. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations revealed the origin of the regioselectivity and the influence of the two trialkylphosphine ligands on borylcupration.

item.title: Accurate modeling of ion-protein binding in solution: molecular mechanics force field innovation and validation on Mg2+
item.description: Multivalent ions bind to proteins to control many biological processes. Molecular simulations can effectively supplement experiments to resolve underlying mechanisms, but reliability and feasibility remain as concerning issues when describing ion-protein binding thermodynamics in the condensed phase. Quantum mechanical (QM) based methods, and now even machine learned force fields, can achieve high accuracy in describing local ion-protein interactions, but either they are prohibitively expensive, or have not been shown to properly describe ion-protein binding in solution. Molecular mechanics (MM) force fields, which are orders-in-magnitude faster than these methods and are used routinely to simulate ion-protein complexes, have not yet been proven to accurately predict ion-protein binding free energies. Here we propose a generalizable approach for achieving high accuracy in MM force fields. Using the divalent Mg2+ as a model, we show that polarizable force fields can achieve QM-level accuracy in local Mg protein interaction energies, with a mean absolute error of 3.3 kcal/mol (0.5%). The Mg-protein binding geometries also match experiment. The Mg-protein binding free energies in solution are also within a couple of kcal/mol from experimental estimates, and the force field is able to thermodynamically distinguish between different chemical binding sites, reproducing the experimentally observed trend in relative binding affinity. Achieving this required improving the electric field responses of ion-coordinating protein chemical groups, including both energetic and structural targets in optimization functions, accounting for interaction energy errors outside the ion’s inner-shell, and accounting for biases in reference energies obtained from quantum mechanical density functional theory. Overall, our work demonstrates that MM force fields are capable of achieving the precision needed for quantitatively studying mechanisms involving ion-protein binding, and lays foundation for future development of MM force fields for other ions. Additionally, our new version of the polarizable AMOEBA-HFC force field opens the way to quantitatively study Mg-dependent mechanisms in hundreds of enzymes and proteins.

item.title: End-to-End Continuous Flow Synthesis of a Bench-Stable Sulfamoylating Reagent: Application to the Preparation of a Key Edoxaban Intermediate
item.description: The N-Boc analogue of the Burgess reagent transfers a sulfamoyl group to amines and alcohols under mild conditions, and its use to install sulfamate and sulfamide motifs is well precedented on laboratory scale. Although these motifs occur in many active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs), industrial use of the reagent is limited for two reasons: it is not amenable to storage, and its precursor, N-Boc-sulfamoyl chloride, is itself labile and forms in a strongly exothermic reaction. Herein, we report an efficient end-to-end continuous flow synthesis of the crystalline, bench-stable analogue N-(tert-butoxycarbonyl)-N-[4-(dimethylazaniumylidene)-1,4dihydropyridin-1-ylsulfonyl]azanide. In a two-stage tubular reactor system, the sulfamoyl chloride is generated at 0–5 °C and trapped in-line with DMAP within a total residence time of about 5 min, giving the product in 71% yield and 99.6% HPLC purity. The utility of the reagent in API synthesis was demonstrated in the batch preparation of an Edoxaban precursor, which in turn enabled a shorter route that uses the flow-generated sulfamoyl chloride directly.

item.title: Can fluorine form triple bonds? Relativistic Multireference Electronic Structure, σ/π Bond-Order Decomposition, and All-Electron vs. ECP Audit of Transition-Metal Monofluorides
item.description: Fluorine is the most electronegative element and is canonically treated as a monovalent σ-acceptor, although partial π-donation is established in NF and CF+. Building on an earlier preprint (DOI 10.26434/chemrxiv2022-xlsjn-v3), I perform a scalar-relativistic all-electron multireference study (X2C-CASSCF/SC-NEVPT2 with cc-pVTZ-DK) of CF+, NF, neutral MnF, and high-valent 3d/4d monofluoride cations using σ/π-decomposed Mayer bond orders and Löwdin populations. For neutral MnF in its X 7Σ + ground state, X2C-CAS(12,9)- NEVPT2 reproduces the experimental bond length (re = 1.8341 Å vs. 1.838 Å) and neon-matrix vibrational frequency (ωe = 606.8 cm−1 vs. 608.5 cm−1 ) as a polar single bond (BO = 0.617, q(F) = −0.339). The closedshell 1Σ + state lies +5.520 eV higher and remains singlebonded (BO = 0.893), while forensic stability checks uncover a −2.94 eV RHF-to-UHF instability in the original preprint. Late-3d trications ([MnF]3+, [NiF]3+) undergo Coulomb explosion before triple bonding emerges, whereas all-electron X2C and def2-TZVP ECP yield opposite bound-versus-repulsive predictions on [PdF]2+ and [PdF]3+. Finally, rational screening of 10-electron main-group and d 0 early-transition-metal cations identifies bound fluorine triple bonds reaching BO = 2.48–2.58 in [WF]5+ and [MoF]5+, and BO = 2.745 (π = 1.85) in [OF]3+

item.title: POLEN: An OpenMM Framework for ML/MM Simulations with Mutually Polarizable AMOEBA Embedding
item.description: Hybrid machine-learning and molecular mechanics formulations have been growing over the years. The attractive cost-effectiveness for big systems (such as protein complexes) has made these methods gain attention in the computational chemistry/biology field. In these theories, one of the most discussed themes is embedding, which can add or remove physics from the system. Here, we present POLEN (POLarizable Embedding for Neural-network potentials), an OpenMM plugin for ML/MM simulations with a mutually polarizable AMOEBA embedding, including a variant whose ML-trained head (MuPE(ML)) predicts multipoles, polarizabilities, and charge penetration at each simulation step. After validating the formulation on N -methylacetamide in water, we applied it to three systems: . . . (CK2α–TBB− , in two binding poses). Against QM/AMOEBA, MuPE(ML) reduces the ligand–environment interaction error from up to 55 to ∼5 kJ mol−1 , and the embedding changes the pNA solvation and the CK2 pose populations. These results show that letting the electrostatics of the ML region follow its geometry in a mutually polarizable environment changes structural outcomes that mechanical and fixed-multipole embeddings miss, at 1.5–2.3 times the cost of mechanical embedding for proteins. POLEN is open source.

item.title: Ligand Connectivity Control of Hubbard Interactions at Metal Sites in Frameworks and Oxides Revealed by Theory-Guided Agents
item.description: Coordination chemistry ranks ligands via the spectrochemical and nephelauxetic series, but both rely on d-d spectra and leave d⁰ metals unranked. Ligands should similarly govern the Hubbard U (on-site Coulomb repulsion) and intersite V (metal-ligand repulsion), which single-U-per-element DFT+U obscures. Here two LLM agents, a Teacher asking from theory and a Student answering from data, propose ligand rules from linear-response data on 241 metal-organic frameworks and 57 oxides, which we establish from response matrices and first-principles calculations. At fixed element, oxidation state and coordination number, the first coordination sphere sets the U of Zr and Hf via metal d–carboxylate O 2p coupling, and V ranks oxygen donors by protonation and bridging mode as a ligand series for d⁰ metals. In iron oxoanion salts, the oxoanion central atom raises Fe U through the same coupling, so a metal site is defined by its donors and each donor by what else it is bonded to. This ligand connectivity explains how capping ligands set the electronic sites of defective frameworks. Tabulated by ligand type, U and V replace linear-response calculations costing about 400 times the ground state and reproduce the DFT+U+V electronic structure of a Zr node within a few meV. Controlled experiments show that theory-guided questions move agents from statistical association to falsifiable mechanistic hypotheses. This work supports high-throughput modelling of charge localization and transfer, rational ligand engineering and physical-chemistry discovery from existing data.

item.title: Checking the checks on quantum-chemical outputs: four open-source tools for stationary points, reaction paths, spectra and slab convergence, tested against independent references
item.description: The numbers that leave a quantum-chemical calculation are usually processed by short scripts that are rarely tested (stationary points, free energies, tunnelling factors, spectra, surface energies). We tested four open-source Python packages that automate such steps, QMCert, NEBCert, SpecCert and CatCert, against independent references: the cclib parser, GoodVibes and the program’s own output (59 ORCA 6.1 calculations); ORCA’s fullprecision files, overreact and a 40-digit reference (12 ORCA nudged-elasticband runs and 720 tunnelling cases); ORCA’s spectrum tool, the NIST CCCBDB scaling-factor table and pymatgen (8 molecules and 9 VASP calculations); and ASE and hand calculations (an Al(111) slab series and H adsorption, Quantum ESPRESSO). The corrected releases reproduce every reference to its printing precision. The tests exposed defects in the first releases that no author-written unit test had caught: a quasi-harmonic correction that invited users to apply it twice (up to 0.73 kcal mol−1), Eckart tunnelling factors wrong by up to 10⁴⁶, a failed job passed as a 71,706 kcal mol−1 barrier, absorption coefficients 24% too low, invented infrared intensities, d-band centres off by up to 0.77 eV, and a surface-energy convergence rule whose verdict depends on where the thickness series stops (PASS at 7 layers, FAIL at 11, on the same calculations). Two optimisations of open-shell molecules converged, with every criterion met, to saddle points. The shared lesson: a check must be tested on real outputs, designed failures and an independent implementation, and its verdict reported with what it did not test.

item.title: Electrons Follow Mysterious Pathways: Cyclic Delocalization versus Electron Sharing
item.description: Which circuit of a polycyclic or macrocyclic molecule carries its aromatic character? Electronic delocalization indices are widely used to answer this question, yet different indices often select different circuits. We trace the origin of these disagreements in two prototypes, coronene and free-base porphyrin. In a representation with one 𝜋 orbital per atom, the ring-ordered (Kekulé) term of the normalized multicenter index, KMCI𝜋, is exactly the geometric mean of the 𝜋 bond orders along the circuit. Strongly shared bonds can therefore compensate for weak ones, and a circuit rich in bonds with strong double-bond character can receive a high value. In coronene, KMCI𝜋 ranks the perimeter first because it contains all six olefinic CH=CH bonds, whereas the full MCI, which adds the cross-ring cyclic orderings, ranks it third, behind the two circuits that the electron density of delocalized bonds (EDDB) also ranks highest. EDDB, which shows the spatial distribution of delocalized electrons, places the perimeter among the least delocalized circuits. In porphyrin, the pyrrolic nitrogen with relatively high lone-pair occupancy shares little with its neighbors, so its 𝜋 bond orders are small. This lowers KMCI𝜋 and the four-center indices AV1245 and AVmin for every circuit through N–H. All three indices therefore favor the [18]annulene-type circuit, which bypasses both N–H groups, and so does the full MCI. The same nitrogen, however, carries a delocalized population comparable to that of the carbon atoms, and the delocalized population of the macrocycle is nearly the same whichever route is taken at N–H (9.7 vs 9.6 e), while its least delocalized atom carries more on the inner route (0.48 vs 0.36 e). Both views are consistent with resonance between Clar structures with migrating 𝜋-sextets. A high ring index therefore does not by itself show that delocalization extends uniformly around the whole circuit. Before such a value is read as a measure of cyclic delocalization, the bonds and atoms that determine it should be identified.

item.title: Iron-Photocatalysed Ligand-to-Metal Charge Transfer Coupled with Nickel-Catalysed SH2 for Decarboxylative sp3–sp3 Coupling of Free Carboxylic Acids and NHPI Esters
item.description: Decarboxylative cross-coupling of two alkyl fragments without precious-metal catalysts, external oxidants, or stoichiometric base remains a central challenge in synthetic chemistry. Here we show that near-UV (395 nm) excitation of an Fe(III)–carboxylate complex initiates decarboxylative sp3–sp3 coupling of free carboxylic acids with N-hydroxyphthalimide (NHPI) redox-active esters by ligand-to-metal charge transfer (LMCT), in cooperation with a nickel catalyst that closes the cycle through bimolecular homolytic substitution (SH2). A single loading of trifluoroethanol (≈0.55 equiv, 4 µL at 0.1 mmol scale) replaces the external base by acting as a proton shuttle between the iron and nickel cycles. Turnover depends on a β-carbonyl handle on at least one coupling partner: the carbonyl chelates nickel in a five-membered ring and stabilises the Ni(III)–alkyl intermediate against β-hydride elimination and hydrogen-atom transfer (HAT) quenching. The platform engages unactivated, long-chain primary alkyl groups at 27–44% (NHPI-ester side) and 14–37% (free-acid side), a regime that remains difficult to reach under purely photochemical, base-free conditions, delivers 39 unique products (41 entries) at 14–96% yield overall, and provides a working hypothesis for the cooperative iron/nickel cycle that remains subject to further mechanistic validation.

item.title: PoseMend: Post-Hoc Repair of Ligand Stereochemistry in Protein–Ligand Docking
item.description: A molecule and its mirror image are different compounds with different biology, so a docking pose that inverts a stereocentre describes the wrong molecule regardless of how accurately it is positioned. We show that susceptibility to this failure—and to a whole class of related failures—is determined by a method’s output parameterisation rather than by its accuracy, its architecture, or whether it is physics-based or learned. The argument is a reachability result, and it generalises. Every operation available to a method that emits a rigid-body placement and torsion angles is a rigid motion of the subtrees it acts on, so such a method cannot alter any quantity fixed by the conformer’s bonded geometry. This partitions a standard validity battery a priori into six checks a torsional method cannot fail—chirality, bond lengths, bond angles, ring planarity, double-bond planarity and double-bond stereochemistry—and three it can, namely those depending on the torsions or the placement it is free to choose. Tested across 24 methods, all six predicted-protected checks separate the two parameterisation classes and none of the three predicted-free checks does (p = 0.012 for the ordering; Fisher combination over the protected set p = 1.7× 10−9). Individually the per-check tests are underpowered at 24 methods: after Holm correction two of the six survive, and we claim the result at the level of the partition rather than per check. A method that emits Cartesian atom coordinates can reach the mirror arrangement; a method that emits a rigid-body placement and torsion angles applied to a graph-built conformer provably cannot, because every such operation has determinant +1 and therefore preserves the sign of the signed chiral volume. Recomputing chirality failure from the released per-method result files of the PoseX benchmark, we find all ten Cartesian-output methods fail on 1.68% to 37.60% of poses while thirteen of fourteen torsion/rigid-body methods fail on 0.00% to 0.29% (Mann–Whitney p = 9.3× 10−5 on self-docking, p = 7.6× 10−5 on cross-docking, with the single counterexample scored against the hypothesis). Per-method rates agree across the two benchmarks at Spearman ρ = 0.941. Guided by this account we introduce POSEMEND, a post-hoc operator that repairs the defect after prediction. It inverts each offending stereocentre by reflecting the smaller substituent subtree—an exact operation on the chiral volume—then relaxes the result under restraints that preserve bond geometry, pocket placement and the receptor clash profile. It has no learned parameters and requires no retraining or access to the predictor. Across five method–benchmark combinations spanning two docking methods and both self-and cross-docking, chirality failure falls from 18.6% to 37.1% to 0.0% to 1.0%. On the largest, Uni-Mol cross-docking (n = 1310), PoseX success rises from 54.50% to 64.50% with 131 targets gained and none lost. On the Astex Diverse Set, held out and pre-registered before use, PoseX success rises from 8.24% to 23.53% (+13 targets, 0 lost, p = 2.4× 10−4) and chirality failure reaches exactly zero. Achiral ligands are returned byte-identical in every set. We further show that the field’s standard post-processing step does not address this defect and can create it: across the ten Cartesian methods, force-field relaxation changes chirality failure by +0.11 *yaiuftuto@gmail.com percentage points on average and improves no method by more than one point, while seven of fourteen torsion/rigid methods acquire stereochemical errors they did not previously have (p = 0.0088)—relaxation being itself a Cartesian operation, it destroys the very invariance that made those methods safe. We report two negative results in full. An earlier version of our own operator silently degraded aromatic ring planarity on up to 8.1% of targets, a regression invisible in the aggregate success rate and detected only by per-check auditing; and the parameterisation account admits one unexplained counterexample, DeepDock, whose optimiser we verify cannot invert a stereocentre yet which fails on 22.98% and 23.02% of poses on the two benchmarks—figures stable to within 0.04 percentage points.

item.title: Overcoming substrate constraints to unlock chiral dihydropyridines for stereodefined piperidine synthesis
item.description: Enantioenriched dihydropyridines provide versatile entry points to stereodefined nitrogen heterocycles. Catalytic asymmetric dearomatization offers an efficient method to access these, but has required electron-withdrawing substituents, limiting accessible structures. Here we report a rhodium-catalyzed asymmetric addition of boronic acids to N-alkylpyridinium salts that removes this requirement. Readily available pyridines react with aryl, heteroaryl and alkenyl boronic acids to afford diverse chiral dihydropyridines in high yields and enantioselectivities, with broad tolerance of substitution patterns and unprotected polar groups. The reaction operates on 100 mmol scale with 0.3 mol% rhodium catalyst, without glovebox handling or chromatography. The products enable divergent synthesis of stereodefined piperidines and complex nitrogen heterocycles, including constitutional isomers for nitrogen-position scanning. This approach substantially expands the accessible chemical space of chiral saturated nitrogen heterocycles.

item.title: Proton Relays Versus Direct Transfer in Polyketide Cyclisations: Solution Rejection, Bioinspired Complexes, and Enzyme-Pocket Rescue
Where Does the Fluorine Go? A Systematic Evidence Audit of Fluorine Fate and Carbon’s Role in PFAS Photocatalysis
item.description: Carbon-containing photocatalysts are proposed for treating per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), but performance is usually reported as parent-compound loss, which does not distinguish adsorption, transformation and C–F bond cleavage. We searched Scopus and Web of Science and audited 115 studies (121 experiments), coding fluorine in six measurable reservoirs and an unresolved fraction, recalculating defluorination and grading evidence for carbon’s electronic role. No study quantified fluorine in all reservoirs: 35 studies measured no fluoride, 12 extracted PFAS from the spent catalyst, one quantified catalyst-bound fluoride and none measured volatile products. Eight of nine numerical fluorine balances covered only the aqueous phase (42–93% recovery); the one including the catalyst recovered 2.35%. Removal exceeded defluorination by a median of 55.8 percentage points when removal included dark adsorption (n = 19) and by 10.4 points when degradation was reported (n = 11); the baseline was not stated for 33 of 63 paired values. Four of twelve recalculable defluorination values did not reproduce, one exceeding the theoretical maximum. The strongest evidence for carbon’s electronic role was correlative charge-carrier data in 67 studies and assertion, calculation or scavenger tests in 40; direct electron transfer to PFAS was shown for two intrinsically photoactive catalysts, neither compared with a carbon-free material. Sixty studies compared carbon-free or carbon-only materials, but none normalized performance to adsorbed PFAS. Carbon’s sorptive functions are well documented; its independent contribution to C–F activation in carbon-supported composites is untested. We propose a four-level reporting standard that separates removal, defluorination, fluorine closure and mechanistic claims.

item.title: Photothermal Nucleophilic Aromatic Substitution via a Traceless Carboxylate Directing Group
item.description: Intermolecular nucleophilic aromatic substitution remains challenging for arenes lacking strong electron-withdrawing groups. Here, we report a photothermal amination–decarboxylation strategy that uses an ortho-carboxylate as a traceless activating group. Under red-light irradiation, inexpensive carbon black enables amination of 2-bromobenzoic acids followed by decarboxylation, providing formal amination products of electronically neutral and electron-rich aryl bromides without transition-metal catalysis. The method accommodates primary aliphatic amines, anilines, and cyclic secondary amines, and its synthetic utility is demonstrated through preparative-scale synthesis and access to pharmaceutically relevant compounds. Competition experiments, substituent correlations, and density functional theory calculations support hydrogen-bond-assisted substitution and implicate steric constraints in the unusual preference for primary over secondary amines. Changing the leaving group from bromide to fluoride reverses this selectivity. Time-course measurements and reactions of a preformed intermediate support sequential substitution and decarboxylation. These findings establish a removable carboxylate activation strategy for extending intermolecular photothermal C–N bond formation beyond strongly activated electrophiles.

item.title: [Re] Simulating micrometer-scale crystal growth from solution
item.description: Piana, Reyhani and Gale (Nature 438, 70; 2005) grew urea crystals in three-dimensional kinetic Monte Carlo simulations driven by site rates counted directly in molecular dynamics, and reproduced the needle shape of urea grown from water and the polar shape grown from methanol. The rates are published in the Supplementary Information; the model that uses them is described briefly. We wrote an independent implementation from the published papers alone and report three things. First, which of the two chain neighbors the rate tables call A depends on whether a rate is read from the point of view of the central molecule or of the arriving one, a point the corresponding author confirmed. Read from the arriving molecule's point of view, the tables give saturation at 4.7 M (water) and 3.4 M (methanol), against the published 5 M and 4 M; read the other way, they give about twice that and no needle. The first reading reproduces the paper's morphological claims: a needle in water whose {110} faces do not grow, pointed methanol ends twisted by 90°, birth-and-spread growth of the methanol {110} face, a methanol shape less elongated than the water one, and steps on {110} that advance about twice as fast one way along c as the other. Second, the published rates are additive in bond energies at equilibrium but not in kinetics, which is what measuring them buys over an energy-based model. Third, exact continuous-time kinetic Monte Carlo and the paper's 50-ps synchronous sweep give the same morphologies. Code and inputs are open.

item.title: ADMET-Engine v2.0: Scaffold-Validated Multi-Modal Graph and QSAR Ensembling with Calibrated Epistemic Uncertainty, Applicability Domain Quantification, and Analytical Pharmacokinetics
item.description: Late-stage attrition in small-molecule drug discovery remains disproportionately driven by off-target cardiotoxicity—chiefly human ether-à-go-go-related gene (HERG/Kv11.1) potassium channel blockade—and hepatic cytochrome P450 3A4 (CYP3A4) drug–drug interactions. Although deep graph neural networks have proliferated in computational toxicology, deployed academic pipelines routinely suffer from four methodological failure modes: (i) random train/test partitioning that leaks congeneric chemical series across splits and inflates apparent ROC-AUC; (ii) uncalibrated raw neural logits misinterpreted as decision probabilities; (iii) absence of explicit applicability domain (AD) verification to warn medicinal chemists against out-of-distribution extrapolation; and (iv) disconnection from deterministic medicinal chemistry rules and structural alert filters. We present ADMET-Engine v2.0, an open-source computational medicinal chemistry framework trained on 16,270 unique standardized CHEMBL v37 compounds under a strict Bemis–Murcko scaffold split (8,252 unique core frameworks; zero core overlap across train, calibration-validation, and held-out test partitions). ADMET-Engine integrates four structurally heterogeneous model families—a Chemprop-grade 45-dimensional one-hot Directed Message-Passing Neural Network (DMPNN) with an O(E) reverse-edge indexing algorithm eliminat-ing O(N2) batch memory blowup, a residual ECFP4+physicochemical deep neural network, an ExtraTrees non-linear QSAR ensemble, and an L2-regularized logistic QSAR classifier—calibrated via validation-set temperature scaling and combined through convex negative log-likelihood optimization. On completely unseen core scaffolds (n = 1,627), the calibrated consensus ensemble achieves ROC-AUC = 0.7836 (PR-AUC = 0.8955, Brier = 0.1656, ECE = 0.0328) on HERG (n = 1,177) and ROC-AUC = 0.7664 (PR-AUC = 0.8506, Brier = 0.1875, ECE = 0.0541) on CYP3A4 (n = 516), improving by +0.216 ROC-AUC over the prior unscaled scalar-feature baseline. Every inference further computes sub-millisecond bit-packed ECFP4 Tanimoto applicability domain diagnostics, weighted epistemic uncertainty (σepi), exact analytical BOILED-EGG gastrointestinal and blood–brain barrier permeation, QED, Fsp3, Pfizer 3/75 promiscuity, and PAINS/BRENK toxicophore atom highlighting on 2D structures.

item.title: Solid-Phase Total Synthesis of Wewakazole B
item.description: Wewakazole B is a cytotoxic cyclododecapeptide isolated from the marine cyanobacterium Moorea producens, containing three embedded oxazole heterocycles derived from serine and threonine residues. Reported total syntheses of Wewakazole B rely exclusively on solution-phase strategies, which are stepintensive and poorly suited to modular analogue generation. Here we report a solid-phase peptide synthesis route to Wewakazole B enabled by custom Fmoc-protected oxazole and methyloxazole amino acid building blocks. These heterocyclic residues were prepared through a modular dipeptide-based route employing DAST-mediated cyclodehydration followed by oxidative aromatization. The building blocks were incorporated directly into Fmoc-SPPS using a combination of automated and manual coupling, avoiding late-stage heterocycle installation. Macrocyclization of the resulting linear precursor, followed by purification via normal-phase chromatography afforded Wewakazole B in 20% overall yield. To our knowledge, this represents the first solid-phase total synthesis of Wewakazole B and establishes a generalizable, building-block-based platform for the synthesis of oxazole-rich cyclic peptides and their structurally defined analogues.

item.title: Digitising Polyoxometalate Syntheses
item.description: Polyoxometalates (POMs) are structurally diverse metal-oxo clusters whose syntheses are governed by a delicate interplay of parameters, including pH, counter-cations, and concentration. To convert this synthetic knowledge into a machine-readable format, we devised a 4-stage automated pipeline. The pipeline employs a series of Large Language Model (LLM) agents for text pre-processing, reagent extraction, and procedure structuring, followed by a final data assembly module to consolidate the outputs. This workflow transformed 405 unstructured synthesis descriptions into a strict JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) corpus containing structured metadata, reagents, and operational steps. The resulting database is ready for rapid querying and data-driven optimisation of new POM materials.

item.title: Circular Fluoride Metallurgy Enabled by the Reverse Deacon Reaction in the Presence of Sodium Fluoride: A Theoretical Study
item.description: Historical and current routes to metals have included the reaction of metal oxides with hydrofluoric acid to produce metal fluorides and subsequent sodiothermic reduction. In this communication, we explore the possibility of regenerating hydrofluoric acid from the byproducts of hydrofluoric acid digestion, molten salt electrolysis, and the sodiothermic reduction of metal fluorides, namely, water, chlorine gas, and sodium fluoride. The rationale for such a process is that the reverse Deacon reaction—which generates hydrochloric acid and oxygen from chlorine and water—is strongly endothermic, while halide exchange between NaF and HCl is exothermic; both reactions are entropically favorable. Thermodynamic modeling suggests that these reactions could be coupled to produce hydrofluoric acid, sodium chloride, and oxygen in good yields across a range of temperatures without the use of carbon reagents. Simulations suggest this reaction could be driven to completion by slight excesses of water and chlorine, allowing the regeneration of hydrofluoric acid with moderate heat requirements. When combined with hydrofluoric acid routes to metal fluorides, molten salt electrolysis of sodium chloride, and sodiothermic reduction of metal fluorides, this novel thermochemical oxygen-generating reaction has the potential to enable circular production of metals and oxygen from metal oxides using fluoride metallurgy.

item.title: Why Applicability Domains Pass Conventional Validation: Close-Neighbour Provenance
item.description: Chemists judge a QSAR prediction by asking whether the molecule resembles the training data. This check is the applicability domain (AD), usually the similarity to the nearest training molecule, and the OECD lists it as a validation principle. We asked whether it still flags bad predictions when the test molecules come from papers the model has never seen. We used 39 ChEMBL targets and three model families. The AUC for flagging errors above one log unit falls from 0.664 with scaffold-disjoint splits to 0.568 when publications are withheld. It falls to 0.494 on future publications. The main cause is where close neighbours come from. In the standard test 55% of molecules have a close training neighbour from their own paper and only 9% have one from another paper. A Butina-0.4 cluster holdout leaves those neighbours in place and the AD does not change. Removing the neighbours, or removing the papers, makes it collapse. The failure is sharper for the pass/fail gate practitioners actually deploy. A permissive 0.35 cutoff separates errors in the standard test (0.144 inside against 0.408 outside) and not on withheld papers (0.372 against 0.362). We also calibrated a cutoff honestly, on a publication-disjoint split. A cutoff promising 15% error cannot be found at all in 7 to 13 of 20 splits. Where it exists it admits 2.3% or fewer of the molecules at about 2 times the promised error. Six similarity metrics and three model-based uncertainty scores all degrade in the same direction. We give a cutoff sweep and a one-number diagnostic. The diagnostic is the share of validation molecules with a close neighbour from a different paper, which is 9% here. It flags validation sets that cannot test reliability on new publications.

item.title: Composition-Dependent Electrochemical Nitrate Reduction Performance of Tungsten Nitride
item.description: Electrochemical reduction of nitrate to ammonia provides a route for coupling nitrogenpollutant remediation with value-added chemical production. However, the multistep reaction network makes catalytic performance sensitive to the electronic structure and intermediate-binding characteristics of the catalyst surface. Here, we systematically tune the nitrogen content of tungsten nitride (WNx) thin-film electrodes by reactive magnetron sputtering and examine how nitrogen incorporation affects phase composition, working electronic state, nitrate-reduction kinetics, and operational stability. Increasing the N2/Ar flow ratio in the sputtering environment gradually drives structural evolution from α-W-containing WNx to β-W2N-rich films, then to δ-WN-rich compositions. In particular, the β-W2N-rich electrode exhibits the highest NH3 production rate, reaching 57 ± 3 mg h–1 cm–2 with an NH3 Faradaic efficiency of 84.5 ± 2.0% at –0.7 VRHE, whereas both lower and higher nitrogen contents result in reduced activity. First-principles calculations reveal distinct W 5d/N 2p hybridization and bonding characteristics in β-W2N and δ-WN. Under operating conditions, in situ W L3-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy shows that nitrogen-rich WNx remains comparatively more oxidized under cathodic polarization. In situ Raman spectroscopy further reveals a stronger and more persistent *NO-related vibrational feature on δ-WN-rich WNx. Along the HNO pathway, free-energy calculations identify an unfavorable *NO-to-*HNO conversion on δ-WN, consistent with the observed *NO accumulation. Repeated potential cycling, post-reaction microscopy, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), and dissolved-W analysis further show that β-W2N-rich WNx is more stable than the δ-WN-rich compositions. These results highlight the importance of nitrogen-content-dependent W-centered electronic states and their evolution under operating conditions in governing nitratereduction activity, intermediate conversion, and electrochemical stability.

item.title: A One-Step, Azide-Free Synthesis of 4-azatricyclo[4.3.1.13,8]undecan-5-one from 2-Adamantone and Single Crystal X-Ray Diffraction Analysis
item.description: We have developed a one-step, azide-free protocol for the multigram preparation of 4-azatricyclo[4.3.1.13,8]undecan-5-one from 2-adamantone. Single crystals of the product were grown by slow evaporation from ethanol and analyzed by X-ray diffraction. The previously reported but structurally uncharacterized HCl adduct was also isolated and structurally characterized, which confirms protonation at the O atom and indicates a pattern of enhanced Brønsted basicity of 7-membered lactams relative to amides in general.

item.title: Programmable Deaminative Functionalization enabled by Nitrate Anion
item.description: Aliphatic amines constitute a vast reservoir of molecular diversity, yet their potential for deaminative functionalization remains largely untapped. Harnessing this resource requires cleaving stable C–N bonds without sacrificing molecular architecture or sensitive functionalities. Here, nitrate-enabled deamination unlocks the direct conversion of complex amines into chlorides for divergent functionalization, extending the synthetic reach beyond the constraints of conventional diazonium chemistry. Our platform transforms valuable bioactive amines into electrophilic linchpins for carbon–heteroatom and carbon–carbon bond formation, with nucleophilic substitutions proceeding without intermediate isolation. The mild conditions preserve acid-sensitive functionalities, including acetals and Boc-protected amines, and accommodate complex molecules and FDA-approved drugs. Gram-scale synthesis and parallel diversification establish the preparative utility and downstream versatility of the platform both in academic and industrial settings.

item.title: DESIGN AND SYNTHESIS OF PYRROLO[2,3-D]PYRIMIDINES AND THIENO[2,3-D]PYRIMIDINES BEARING A 5-(PIPERAZIN-1-YLSULFONYL)-1,3-OXAZOLE-4-CARBONITRILE MOIETY
